imc-2009-01.title: Counterexample and density
imc-2009-01.body:
**(a) No.** Let $f$ be the indicator function of $[\sqrt3,\infty)$ and $g$ the indicator function of $(\sqrt3,\infty)$:
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x\ge\sqrt3\\0,&x<\sqrt3\end{cases}\qquad g(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x>\sqrt3\\0,&x\le\sqrt3.\end{cases}$$
Both are non-decreasing. They differ only at the irrational point $\sqrt3$, so $f(r)=g(r)$ for every rational $r$; but $f(\sqrt3)=1>0=g(\sqrt3)$.

**(b) Yes.** Let $h=g-f$; it is continuous and $h(r)\ge0$ for all rational $r$. Take any real $x$ and a sequence of rationals $r_k\to x$ (rationals are dense). By continuity $h(x)=\lim_k h(r_k)\ge0$, because a limit of non-negative numbers is non-negative. Hence $f(x)\le g(x)$.

Equivalently: if $h(x)<0$ for some $x$, continuity gives an interval around $x$ on which $h<0$; this interval contains a rational $r$ with $h(r)<0$, a contradiction.

**Answer: (a) no; (b) yes.** ∎

imc-2009-02.title: Find an inverse of $A-B$
imc-2009-02.body:
Let $I$ be the identity matrix. Since $(A-B)A^{-1}=I-BA^{-1}$,
$$(A-B)(C+A^{-1})=(A-B)C+I-BA^{-1}.$$
By hypothesis $(A-B)C=BA^{-1}$, so the right-hand side equals $I$:
$$(A-B)(C+A^{-1})=I.$$
For square matrices, $XY=I$ implies $YX=I$ (indeed $\det X\det Y=1$, so $X$ is invertible and $Y=X^{-1}$). Hence also
$$(C+A^{-1})(A-B)=I,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad CA-CB+I-A^{-1}B=I .$$
Cancelling $I$ gives $C(A-B)=CA-CB=A^{-1}B$. ∎

imc-2009-03.title: Count walks of length 2
imc-2009-03.body:
Let $G$ be the friendship graph: vertices are residents, edges are friendships. Then $a_i=\deg v_i$, any two non-adjacent vertices have a common neighbour, no vertex has degree $n-1$, and $k$ is the length of the shortest cycle of $G$ (its *girth*).

**Walks of length 2.** A walk of length 2 is an ordered triple $(u,w,v)$ with $uw$ and $wv$ edges ($u=v$ allowed). For a fixed middle vertex $w$ there are $\deg(w)^2$ of them, so there are $\sum a_i^2=n^2-n$ such walks in total.

**An injection.** For each ordered pair $(u,v)$ of distinct vertices define a walk $\Phi(u,v)$: if $uv$ is an edge, $\Phi(u,v)=(u,v,u)$; otherwise choose a common neighbour $w$ and put $\Phi(u,v)=(u,w,v)$. A walk with distinct ends $(u,w,v)$ can only be $\Phi(u,v)$, and a walk $(u,v,u)$ can only be $\Phi(u,v)$; so $\Phi$ is injective. There are $n^2-n$ ordered pairs, so $\sum a_i^2\ge n^2-n$, and in our case **equality holds, so $\Phi$ is a bijection**. Consequences:

* *No triangles.* If $u,w,v$ formed a triangle, the walk $(u,w,v)$ would have to be $\Phi(u,v)$; but $uv$ is an edge, so $\Phi(u,v)=(u,v,u)\neq(u,w,v)$. Contradiction.
* *No 4-cycles.* If $u\,w\,v\,w'$ were a 4-cycle, then $u,v$ are non-adjacent (no triangles), and both $(u,w,v)$ and $(u,w',v)$ would have to equal $\Phi(u,v)$. Contradiction.

So every cycle of $G$ has length at least $5$.

**$G$ has a cycle.** Otherwise $G$ is a forest; it is connected because any two vertices are at distance at most $2$, so it is a tree. ($n\ge3$: for $n\le2$ some vertex would be adjacent to all others.) Take a leaf $\ell$ and its neighbour $c$. For any vertex $x\neq \ell,c$ the unique path from $\ell$ to $x$ passes through $c$ and has length $\le2$, so $x$ is adjacent to $c$. Then $\deg c=n-1$, which is forbidden.

**The shortest cycle has length exactly 5.** We use:

*Lemma.* If two different paths join the same vertices $x$ and $y$, their union contains a cycle of length at most the sum of their lengths.
*Proof.* Walk along the first path from $x$; let $a$ be the last vertex before the paths first separate, and let $b$ be the first vertex after $a$ on the first path that lies on the second path (it exists since $y$ is on both). The piece of the first path from $a$ to $b$ and the piece of the second path between $a$ and $b$ have only $a,b$ in common, so together they form a cycle, of length at most the total length. $\square$

Let $C$ be a shortest cycle, of length $k\ge5$, and suppose $k\ge6$. Pick vertices $x,y$ on $C$ at distance $3$ along $C$; the two arcs of $C$ between them have lengths $3$ and $k-3\ge3$. Since $d_G(x,y)\le2$, there is a path $P$ from $x$ to $y$ of length $\le2$; it differs from the arc of length $3$. By the lemma their union contains a cycle of length at most $2+3=5<k$, a contradiction. Hence $k=5$.

**$k=5$ occurs.** The 5-cycle $C_5$: each vertex has 2 friends (not everyone), two non-adjacent vertices have a common neighbour, and $\sum a_i^2=5\cdot4=20=5^2-5$. Its girth is $5$.

**Answer: $k=5$ is the only possible value.** ∎

imc-2009-04.title: A non-negative convolution kernel
imc-2009-04.body:
By the maximum modulus principle, the maximum of $|p|$ and of $|q|$ over the closed unit disc is attained on the circle $|z|=1$. Write $M_f=\max_{|z|=1}|f(z)|$; we must show $M_q\le M_p$. If $n=0$ then $q=p$; assume $n\ge1$.

**Step 1: we may assume $c_n=0$.** If $c_n=1$ all $c_j=1$ and $q=p$. Otherwise put $c'_j=\frac{c_j-c_n}{1-c_n}$. This sequence again satisfies $1=c'_0\ge\dots\ge c'_n=0$ and is convex (it is a positive multiple of $c_j$ minus a constant). Let $r(z)=\sum_j c'_ja_jz^j$. Then $c_n a_j+(1-c_n)c'_ja_j=c_ja_j$, i.e. $q=c_np+(1-c_n)r$. If the claim holds for sequences ending in $0$, then $M_r\le M_p$ and
$$M_q\le c_nM_p+(1-c_n)M_r\le M_p .$$

**Step 2: an integral formula.** For integers $j$,
$$\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}p(e^{i\theta})e^{-ij\theta}\,d\theta=\begin{cases}a_j,&0\le j\le n,\\0,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
since $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(m-j)\theta}d\theta=2\pi[m=j]$. Hence for $|w|=1$,
$$q(w)=\sum_{j=-n}^{n}c_{|j|}w^j\cdot\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}p(e^{i\theta})e^{-ij\theta}d\theta=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}K\!\left(we^{-i\theta}\right)p(e^{i\theta})\,d\theta,$$
where $K(u)=\sum_{j=-n}^nc_{|j|}u^j$ (the terms with $j<0$ contribute $0$). For $|u|=1$, $K(u)=c_0+2\sum_{j\ge1}c_j\,\mathrm{Re}(u^j)$ is real, and $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}K(e^{it})\,dt=c_0=1$.

**Step 3: $K\ge0$ on the unit circle.** With $c_n=0$ set $c_{n+1}=0$ and $d_k=c_{k-1}-2c_k+c_{k+1}$ for $1\le k\le n$. For $k\le n-1$, $d_k\ge0$ by convexity, and $d_n=c_{n-1}\ge0$. Let $\Delta_k=c_{k-1}-c_k$, so $d_k=\Delta_k-\Delta_{k+1}$ and $\Delta_{n+1}=0$. Summation by parts gives, for $0\le j\le n$,
$$\sum_{k=j+1}^{n}(k-j)d_k=\sum_{k=j+1}^{n}\Delta_k=c_j-c_n=c_j .$$
Therefore
$$K(u)=\sum_{|j|\le n}\ \sum_{k>|j|}(k-|j|)d_k\,u^j=\sum_{k=1}^nd_kF_k(u),\qquad F_k(u)=\sum_{|j|\le k-1}(k-|j|)u^j .$$
For $|u|=1$ we have $\bar u=u^{-1}$, and since the number of pairs $(a,b)\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}^2$ with $a-b=j$ is $k-|j|$,
$$F_k(u)=\Big(\sum_{a=0}^{k-1}u^a\Big)\Big(\sum_{b=0}^{k-1}u^{-b}\Big)=\Big|1+u+\dots+u^{k-1}\Big|^2\ge0 .$$
So $K(u)\ge0$ on the circle.

**Step 4: conclusion.** For $|w|=1$,
$$|q(w)|\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}K(we^{-i\theta})\,|p(e^{i\theta})|\,d\theta\le M_p\cdot\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}K(we^{-i\theta})\,d\theta=M_p,$$
using $K\ge0$ and the rotation invariance of the integral. Hence $M_q\le M_p$. ∎

imc-2009-05.title: Barycentric coordinates and inner products
imc-2009-05.body:
**Volumes.** Write $P=\sum_{i}\lambda_iP_i$ with $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$ (barycentric coordinates); since $P$ is inside $S$, all $\lambda_i>0$. The volume of a simplex with vertices $Q_0,\dots,Q_n$ is $\frac1{n!}\left|\det M\right|$, where $M$ is the $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix with columns $\binom{1}{Q_j}$. Replacing the column of $P_i$ by $\binom1P=\sum_k\lambda_k\binom1{P_k}$ and using multilinearity (the terms with $k\ne i$ have a repeated column) multiplies the determinant by $\lambda_i$. Hence $v(S_i)=\lambda_iv(S)>0$; in particular each $S_i$ is a genuine simplex, and $\sum_iv(S_i)=v(S)$.

Because $\sum_iv(S_i)=v(S)$, the identity to be proved is unchanged if we translate all points by the same vector. So place the origin at $O=C(S)$, and let $R$ be the circumradius: $|P_j|=R$ for all $j$. It suffices to show
$$X:=\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_iO_i=0,\qquad O_i:=C(S_i).$$

**Equations for $O_i$.** Let $\rho_i$ be the circumradius of $S_i$. For $j\ne i$, $|O_i-P_j|^2=\rho_i^2$ gives $\langle O_i,P_j\rangle=s_i$, where $s_i=\tfrac12\left(|O_i|^2+R^2-\rho_i^2\right)$ does not depend on $j$. Also $|O_i-P|^2=\rho_i^2$ gives
$$\langle O_i,P\rangle=\tfrac12\left(|O_i|^2+|P|^2-\rho_i^2\right)=s_i-\tfrac h2,\qquad h:=R^2-|P|^2 .$$
On the other hand, from $P=\sum_k\lambda_kP_k$,
$$\langle O_i,P\rangle=\sum_{k\ne i}\lambda_ks_i+\lambda_i\langle O_i,P_i\rangle=(1-\lambda_i)s_i+\lambda_i\langle O_i,P_i\rangle .$$
Comparing, $\lambda_i\langle O_i,P_i\rangle=\lambda_is_i-\tfrac h2$.

**Computing $\langle X,P_j\rangle$.** For each $j$,
$$\langle X,P_j\rangle=\sum_{i\ne j}\lambda_i\langle O_i,P_j\rangle+\lambda_j\langle O_j,P_j\rangle=\sum_{i\ne j}\lambda_is_i+\lambda_js_j-\tfrac h2=\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_is_i-\tfrac h2,$$
which does not depend on $j$. Therefore $\langle X,P_j-P_0\rangle=0$ for $j=1,\dots,n$. The vectors $P_j-P_0$ span $\mathbb R^n$ (the vertices are not in a common hyperplane), so $X$ is orthogonal to all of $\mathbb R^n$, i.e. $X=0=C(S)$.

Multiplying $\sum_i\lambda_iC(S_i)=C(S)$ by $v(S)$ gives
$$\sum_{i=0}^nv(S_i)C(S_i)=v(S)C(S). \qquad ∎$$

imc-2009-06.title: Recognise an ellipsoid
imc-2009-06.body:
Choose coordinates with $\ell$ the $z$-axis and $P=(d,0,0)$. For $X=(x,y,z)$ the distance to $\ell$ is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $|XP|=\sqrt{(x-d)^2+y^2+z^2}$. Both are non-negative, so the condition is equivalent to the squared one:
$$x^2+y^2\ge4\left((x-d)^2+y^2+z^2\right)\iff 3x^2-8dx+4d^2+3y^2+4z^2\le0 .$$
Completing the square, $3x^2-8dx=3\left(x-\tfrac43d\right)^2-\tfrac{16}3d^2$, so with $x_1=x-\tfrac43d$:
$$3x_1^2+3y^2+4z^2\le\tfrac43d^2\iff\left(\frac{x_1}{2d/3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{y}{2d/3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{z}{d/\sqrt3}\right)^2\le1 .$$
This is a solid ellipsoid with semi-axes $\tfrac{2d}3,\tfrac{2d}3,\tfrac d{\sqrt3}$, whose volume is
$$\frac43\pi\cdot\frac{2d}3\cdot\frac{2d}3\cdot\frac d{\sqrt3}=\frac{16\pi d^3}{27\sqrt3}=\frac{16\sqrt3\,\pi d^3}{81}.$$
**Answer: $\dfrac{16\pi d^3}{27\sqrt3}$.**

imc-2009-06.title: Integrate the cross-sections
imc-2009-06.body:
From $3x_1^2+3y^2+4z^2\le\frac43d^2$ (derived as in the first solution), the slice at height $z$ is the disc $x_1^2+y^2\le\frac49d^2-\frac43z^2$, non-empty for $|z|\le d/\sqrt3$, with area $\pi\left(\frac49d^2-\frac43z^2\right)$. Hence, with $h=d/\sqrt3$,
$$V=\pi\int_{-h}^{h}\left(\frac49d^2-\frac43z^2\right)dz=\pi\left(\frac89d^2h-\frac89h^3\right)=\frac{8\pi h}{9}\left(d^2-\frac{d^2}3\right)=\frac{16\pi d^3}{27\sqrt3}.$$
**Answer: $\dfrac{16\pi d^3}{27\sqrt3}$.**

imc-2009-07.title: Factor the differential operator
imc-2009-07.body:
Rewrite the hypothesis as $\left(f''-2f'\right)-3\left(f'-2f\right)\ge0$. Put $g=f'-2f$; then $g$ is differentiable, $g(0)=f'(0)-2f(0)=-2$, and
$$g'(x)-3g(x)\ge0\qquad(x\ge0).$$
Hence $\left(g(x)e^{-3x}\right)'=\left(g'(x)-3g(x)\right)e^{-3x}\ge0$, so $g(x)e^{-3x}$ is non-decreasing on $[0,\infty)$ and
$$g(x)e^{-3x}\ge g(0)=-2,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad f'(x)-2f(x)\ge-2e^{3x}\quad(x\ge0).$$
Multiply by $e^{-2x}>0$:
$$\left(f(x)e^{-2x}\right)'=\left(f'(x)-2f(x)\right)e^{-2x}\ge-2e^{x},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\left(f(x)e^{-2x}+2e^{x}\right)'\ge0 .$$
Thus $f(x)e^{-2x}+2e^x$ is non-decreasing on $[0,\infty)$ and
$$f(x)e^{-2x}+2e^x\ge f(0)+2=3 .$$
Multiplying by $e^{2x}$ gives $f(x)\ge3e^{2x}-2e^{3x}$ for all $x\ge0$. ∎

(Note that $3e^{2x}-2e^{3x}$ is exactly the solution of $y''-5y'+6y=0$ with $y(0)=1$, $y'(0)=0$, so the bound is sharp.)

imc-2009-08.title: Traces of powers
imc-2009-08.body:
Let $X=AB-BA$. **$X$ commutes with $A$:**
$$AX-XA=(A^2B-ABA)-(ABA-BA^2)=A^2B+BA^2-2ABA=0 .$$
Hence for every $m\ge0$, $X^mA=AX^m$ and
$$X^{m+1}=X^m(AB-BA)=AX^mB-X^mBA=A(X^mB)-(X^mB)A .$$
Since $\operatorname{tr}(UV)=\operatorname{tr}(VU)$, we get $\operatorname{tr}X^{m+1}=0$ for all $m\ge0$.

Let $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ be the eigenvalues of $X$ (with multiplicity). Then the power sums $p_k=\sum_i\mu_i^k=\operatorname{tr}X^k$ vanish for $k=1,\dots,n$. By Newton's identities $ke_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i$, all elementary symmetric polynomials $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of the $\mu_i$ vanish, so the characteristic polynomial of $X$ is $t^n$. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem $X^n=0$, so $k=n$ works. ∎

imc-2009-08.title: The commutator as a derivation
imc-2009-08.body:
Fix $A$ and define the linear map $\Delta(Y)=AY-YA$ on $M_n(\mathbb C)$. It satisfies the Leibniz rule $\Delta(YZ)=\Delta(Y)Z+Y\Delta(Z)$, and the hypothesis says exactly
$$\Delta^2(B)=A(AB-BA)-(AB-BA)A=A^2B-2ABA+BA^2=0 .$$
Let $X=\Delta(B)=AB-BA$; so $\Delta(X)=0$.

Iterating the Leibniz rule, $\Delta^k(Y_1Y_2\cdots Y_j)$ is the sum, over all ways of distributing the $k$ applications of $\Delta$ among the $j$ factors, of the corresponding products (with multinomial multiplicities). Apply this to $B^j=B\cdots B$:

* if $j<k$, every distribution gives some factor $\Delta^{\ge2}(B)=0$, so $\Delta^k(B^j)=0$; also $\Delta^k(I)=0$;
* if $j=k$, the only surviving terms give each factor exactly one $\Delta$; there are $k!$ such orderings, each equal to $X^k$. So $\Delta^k(B^k)=k!\,X^k$.

By Cayley–Hamilton, $B^n=\alpha_0I+\alpha_1B+\dots+\alpha_{n-1}B^{n-1}$ for some scalars $\alpha_i$. Applying $\Delta^n$ and using the first bullet, $\Delta^n(B^n)=0$. By the second bullet, $n!\,X^n=0$, so $(AB-BA)^n=0$. ∎

imc-2009-09.title: Polynomials as permutations of $\mathbb F_p$
imc-2009-09.body:
**Polynomials of degree $<p$ are functions.** Let $R$ be the set of polynomials over $\mathbb F_p$ of degree $<p$. Every function $\mathbb F_p\to\mathbb F_p$ is given by exactly one element of $R$ (Lagrange interpolation gives existence; two such polynomials agreeing at $p$ points have a difference of degree $<p$ with $p$ roots, so they are equal). Since $a^p=a$ for $a\in\mathbb F_p$, reducing modulo $x^p-x$ does not change the function a polynomial defines. So the operation in the definition of $W$ corresponds exactly to composing functions: $r$ is the element of $R$ representing $h_1\circ h_2$.

**The two generators are permutations.** $f_1(x)=x+1$ is the cyclic permutation $\sigma:0\to1\to\dots\to p-1\to0$. For $f_2(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}x^j+x$: if $a\ne0,1$, then $\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}a^j=\frac{a^{p-1}-1}{a-1}=0$ by Fermat, so $f_2(a)=a$; $f_2(1)=(p-1)+1=0$; $f_2(0)=1$. So $f_2$ is the transposition $\tau=(0\ 1)$. (For $p=2$ it equals $x+1$.) Both lie in $R$.

**$W$ consists of permutation polynomials.** Let $W'$ be the set of all elements of $R$ that define permutations of $\mathbb F_p$. It contains $f_1,f_2$ and is closed under the operation (a composition of permutations is a permutation). By minimality, $W\subseteq W'$.

**Every permutation occurs.** The functions defined by elements of $W$ form a set closed under composition containing $\sigma$ and $\tau$. Now $\sigma^k\tau\sigma^{-k}=(k\ \ k+1)$, and adjacent transpositions generate the symmetric group $S_p$ (any arrangement can be sorted by adjacent swaps). In a finite group, inverses are positive powers ($g^{-1}=g^{\operatorname{ord}g-1}$), so every element of $S_p$ is a composition of copies of $\sigma$ and $\tau$. Hence every permutation is defined by some element of $W$, i.e. $W'\subseteq W$.

So $W=W'$, which is in bijection with $S_p$: **$|W|=p!$**. ∎

imc-2009-10.title: Evaluation maps and a perturbation lemma
imc-2009-10.body:
Write $X=\mathbb R^p$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$ and regard elements of $T$ as linear maps $X\to Y$. For $x\in X$ let $\mu_x:T\to Y$, $\mu_x(\tau)=\tau(x)$. "Covering" means $\ker\mu_x\ne0$ for every $x$. The column space of $T$ is $\operatorname{span}\{\tau(x):\tau\in T,\ x\in X\}$.

### (a)

Let $T$ be minimal covering, $n=\dim T$, and $U=\{x\in X:\dim\ker\mu_x=1\}$.

**Claim 1. The lines $\ker\mu_x$ ($x\in U$) span $T$.** If not, they lie in a subspace $T'\subset T$ of dimension $n-1$. Then $T'$ is covering: for $x\in U$, $\ker\mu_x\subseteq T'$ is non-zero; for $x\notin U$, $\dim\ker\mu_x\ge2$, so $\dim(\ker\mu_x\cap T')\ge2+(n-1)-n=1$. This contradicts minimality.

**Claim 2 (Lemma).** If $x_0\in U$, $\ker\mu_{x_0}=\mathbb R\tau_0$, and $x\in X$, then $\tau_0(x)=\tau(x_0)$ for some $\tau\in T$; i.e. $\tau_0(x)\in V:=\operatorname{Im}\mu_{x_0}$.

*Proof.* $\dim V=n-1$. Choose a complement $T=\mathbb R\tau_0\oplus T_1$; then $\mu_{x_0}$ maps $T_1$ isomorphically onto $V$. Suppose $w:=\tau_0(x)\notin V$. Define, for $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$, the linear map
$$\Phi_\varepsilon:\mathbb R\times T_1\to Y,\qquad (a,\sigma)\mapsto aw+\sigma(x_0)+\varepsilon\,\sigma(x).$$
$\Phi_0$ is injective ($aw+\sigma(x_0)=0$ with $w\notin V$ forces $a=0$, then $\sigma=0$). Injectivity means some $n\times n$ minor of the matrix of $\Phi_\varepsilon$ is non-zero; minors depend continuously on $\varepsilon$, so $\Phi_\varepsilon$ is injective for all small $|\varepsilon|$. For such $\varepsilon\neq0$ and $\tau=a\tau_0+\sigma$:
$$\tau(x_0+\varepsilon x)=\varepsilon a\,w+\sigma(x_0)+\varepsilon\sigma(x)=\Phi_\varepsilon(\varepsilon a,\sigma),$$
using $\tau_0(x_0)=0$. So $\tau(x_0+\varepsilon x)=0$ forces $\varepsilon a=0$, $\sigma=0$, i.e. $\tau=0$: no non-zero element of $T$ kills $x_0+\varepsilon x$, contradicting the covering property. $\square$

**Counting.** By Claim 1 pick $x_1,\dots,x_n\in U$ and $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_n$ with $\ker\mu_{x_i}=\mathbb R\tau_i$ and $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_n$ a basis of $T$. Extend to a spanning family $x_1,\dots,x_d$ of $X$. Put $y_{ij}=\tau_i(x_j)$; these span the column space of $T$, and $y_{ii}=0$. By the lemma (with $x_0=x_i$, $\tau_0=\tau_i$, $x=x_j$), for all $i,j$,
$$y_{ij}=\tau(x_i)\ \text{ for some }\tau=\textstyle\sum_kc_k\tau_k,\qquad\text{so}\qquad y_{ij}\in\operatorname{span}\{y_{ki}:k=1,\dots,n\}. \tag{$*$}$$
Let $Z=\operatorname{span}\{y_{ab}:1\le b<a\le n\}$, of dimension $\le\binom n2$. We show by induction on $i$ that $y_{ij}\in Z$ for all $j$. For $i=1$: by $(*)$, $y_{1j}$ is a combination of $y_{k1}$, $k\ge2$ (as $y_{11}=0$), which lie in $Z$. For general $i$: by $(*)$, $y_{ij}$ is a combination of the $y_{ki}$; those with $k>i$ are in $Z$, $y_{ii}=0$, and those with $k<i$ are in $Z$ by the induction hypothesis. Hence the column space equals $Z$ and $\delta(T)\le\binom n2$.

### (b)

(For $n=1$ there is nothing to construct in a meaningful sense: a one-dimensional $T=\mathbb RA$ is covering only if $\ker A=\mathbb R^p$, i.e. $A=0$; so take $n\ge2$.) Let $p=n$, $m=\binom n2$, rows indexed by pairs $(i,j)$, $1\le i<j\le n$. For $u\in\mathbb R^n$ let $A(u)$ be the matrix with
$$A(u)_{(i,j),j}=u_i,\qquad A(u)_{(i,j),i}=-u_j,\qquad\text{other entries }0,$$
so $(A(u)v)_{(i,j)}=u_iv_j-u_jv_i$. For $u\ne0$, $A(u)v=0$ iff all $2\times2$ minors of $(u\ v)$ vanish iff $v\in\mathbb Ru$; thus $\ker A(u)=\mathbb Ru$. Let $T=\{A(u):u\in\mathbb R^n\}$; $u\mapsto A(u)$ is linear and injective, so $\dim T=n$.

* *Covering:* every $v\ne0$ lies in $\ker A(v)$, and $0$ lies in every kernel.
* *Minimal:* a proper subspace of $T$ is $\{A(u):u\in U'\}$ for a proper subspace $U'\subset\mathbb R^n$, and the union of its kernels is $\bigcup_{u\in U'\setminus0}\mathbb Ru=U'\ne\mathbb R^n$.
* *$\delta(T)=\binom n2$:* for $i<j$, column $j$ of $A(e_i)$ has entry $1$ in row $(i,j)$ and $0$ elsewhere, so all $\binom n2$ standard basis vectors of $\mathbb R^m$ are columns. ∎
